name: Gã
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Campbell, Akua Asantewaa. 2017. A Grammar of Gã. PhD dissertation, Rice University (Houston). 721 pp. hdl.handle.net/1911/102269 (Rice Digital Scholarship Archive PDF).
catalog_locator: sec. 2.1.2 'The phonological word', p. 41 (stress statement); sec. 1.8.4 'Tone', pp. 33-35 (tone system).
catalog_quote: In many languages, especially Indo-European languages, stress is a reliable marker of phonological words. This is because the placement of stress in such languages is predictable, always falling on a syllable in a particular position. As is the case in many tone languages of West Africa, stress does not play a significant role at the word level and is therefore unhelpful in determining phonological words. For instance, Dakubu (1981:235) finds that in Gã, as in Yoruba, the domain of semantically based syllable stress is not the word but the pause group (i.e. the intonation unit). [p. 41] ... Tone plays a very important role in Gã. The language has both lexical and grammatical tone. It has two phonemic tones: High (H) and Low (L). ... Phonetically, there are three tone distinctions: High, Low and Downstepped High (!H). ... The presence of automatic downstep makes Gã a terrace-level tone language. [p. 33]
world_status: statement found in an open source

As is the case in many tone languages of West Africa, stress does not play a significant role at the word level and is therefore unhelpful in determining phonological words. For instance, Dakubu (1981:235) finds that in Gã, as in Yoruba, the domain of semantically based syllable stress is not the word but the pause group (i.e. the intonation unit).'), immediately before heading 2.1.3 The grammatical word…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ga is a two-tone (H/L, with downstepped H; terrace-level) language. Word-level stress plays no significant role and does not mark the phonological word; what stress there is ('semantically based syllable stress', i.e. emphasis/prominence) is a property of the pause group / intonation unit, not of the word (Campbell citing Dakubu 1981:235). No word-stress position is given because none is claimed.
new_statements.exceptions: None in Campbell. Older contrary-looking statement: Zimmermann 1858 §4 (pp. 5-6) says word 'accentuation' is 'generally on the root of the word and in compound words.. on the fundamental component', and the possessive pronoun takes the accent over its noun; but Zimmermann himself says the accent/intonation systems were 'not yet sufficiently ascertained', and his 'accent' predates tonal analysis.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain explicitly the pause group / intonation unit (phrase level), not the word; statement is about running speech, not citation forms. Alternative reading label: phrase-level prominence only. The word-level claim ('stress does not play a significant role at the word level') is Campbell's own; the pause-group finding is attributed to Dakubu 1981, which was not opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Campbell 2017 describes Gã as spoken in Accra (the standard/central variety; she notes dialects in 1.3.1 but the description is not dialect-specific); Zimmermann 1858 describes the same Accra ('Akra') Gã of the 1850s. Both = gaaa1244; no differently named variety involved.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Gã is a tone language (two phonemic tones H and L, phonetically also downstepped H). Stress does not play a significant role at the word level; following Dakubu 1981, whatever 'semantically based syllable stress' exists has the pause group (intonation unit) as its domain, not the word. No fixed word-stress position exists.

Berry & Kotei 1969 and Campbell 2017 describe standard spoken Gã of Accra (Campbell's data are from Accra speakers; Berry & Kotei aim at 'modern spoken Ga').

tone_statements.quote: The language makes use of both lexical and grammatical tone (Kropp Dakubu 2002). There is a two-way surface contrast between L and H (Table 1). The tone-bearing unit (TBU) is the mora. [...] This two-way surface contrast reflects an underlying three-way distinction between toneless (∅), L and H. This three-way contrast is made clear with verbs once grammatical tone is involved, as toneless verbs pattern with L verbs in some contexts but with H verbs in others (Table 2). In the perfective, which is marked by a floating L tone prefix, toneless verbs pattern with L verbs. However, in the imperative, marked by a floating H tone suffix, toneless verbs pattern with H verbs.
tone_statements.n_tones: 2 surface (H, L; plus downstepped H), 3-way underlying (H, L, toneless)

sources.note: Gã has lexical and grammatical tone; two-way surface contrast H vs L, TBU = mora; underlying three-way contrast H / L / toneless revealed by grammatical tone (perfective = floating L prefix, imperative = floating H suffix); downstepped H from floating L; HL contours only phrase-finally on some CVV verbs and before progressive N-; analyses STAMP (subject-TAM-polarity) portmanteaux as regular tone association + hiatus resolution, incl. vowel-length alternations.
